## [2026-10-22](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-22.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29999>)

EPIC limits policy drift over generated prefixes instead of clipping each token independently or treating a whole response as one unit. Its probability-calibrated prefix objective improves benchmark-selected mathematical reasoning in the tested off-policy mixture-of-experts setup without storing expert-routing decisions, offering an alternative to routing replay.

**Published:** 2026-10-21 · **First seen:** 2026-10-22T10:05:14.945Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Off-policy Reinforcement Learning, Prefix Trust Regions, Mixture of Experts

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.29999v1>) · [Code](<https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Pinned v1 Section 3 (prefix change of measure, exact-KL coordinates and practical objective), the main experiments and relevant implementation/ablation appendices inspected, together with the author repository, pinned initial README and current IMPLEMENTATION.md. EPIC starts from cumulative prefix importance ratios and the reverse-KL coordinate r - 1 - log(r); practical clipping budgets depend on prefix length and geometric mean behavior probability. It uses a geometric-mean ratio, detached prefix weights with current-token-only gradients, sign-aware clipping and implementation log-weight caps. The exact identity does not make the resulting optimization surrogate a hard distribution-level KL constraint. Main experiments train Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base on 17,917 processed DAPO-Math entries with 32 A100 GPUs, 300 steps, 64 prompts times 8 responses per rollout, eight minibatches and one PPO epoch, comparing six methods over three independent training runs. Evaluation uses 130 distinct questions across AIME 2024/2025, AMC 2023 and HMMT February 2025, with eight responses per question. Mean@8 averages binary correctness over the samples; it is not pass@8. Table 1 reports a four-benchmark average of 39.34% for EPIC versus 35.45% for DAPO, the strongest comparison average, and 32.84% for GSPO. Each run selects its best checkpoint using this same four-benchmark average, so these are benchmark-selected results. The separate routing-replay study reports 77.5% and 93.0% lower driver-process CPU resident memory than its R2 and R3 implementations, respectively; these are not GPU-memory or whole-cluster reductions. The original paper receipt is October 21 16:37:09 UTC and its original new-submission announcement is October 22. An inspected initial implementation commit, authored and committed October 20 07:41:35 UTC, already contains the core method/configurations, within the 72-hour lookback. Repository dates do not establish when it became public. This is conservatively newly-discovered catch-up on first inspection today rather than a claim that the paper announcement was the first public release; there is no evidence for an indexing-delay explanation.

**Limitations:** Evidence is one MoE model family, a mathematical-verifier training corpus and one off-policy update configuration. Best checkpoints are selected on the same small benchmark set used for reporting, without a separate held-out checkpoint-selection set, which can bias the reported comparison upward. Main results average three runs but do not establish broad task or model generalization. The practical clipping surrogate and gradient approximations do not guarantee exact distribution-level KL control or monotonic policy improvement. CPU RSS savings depend on routing-index types and the compared implementation, and do not imply a measured end-to-end throughput gain. Comparison clipping settings are not an exhaustive per-method tuning study. No independent reproduction.

## [2026-10-18](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-18.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22324>)

After supervised warm-starting, this recipe trains an 8B model to generate three scientific ideas in one rollout and rewards each idea’s judged quality multiplied by its difference from earlier ideas. The resulting sets outperform quality-only RL on the authors’ document-grounded benchmark, suggesting a practical way to discourage duplicate proposals while leaving scientific validity and source grounding as separate checks.

**Published:** 2026-10-15 · **First seen:** 2026-10-18T21:41:55.857Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Set-level RL, Scientific Ideation, Quality-Diversity Rewards

**Public availability:** 2026-10-16T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22324>) · [Project](<https://github.com/ManyaWadhwa/diverge_ideation>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Full primary HTML, including the reward, training, judging, human-study and execution appendices, inspected. Sections 2–6, Equations 2 and 7, Tables 1, 3, 4 and 11, and Appendices B–F describe one K=3 rollout, a shared GRPO set advantage, a quality-times-nearest-prior-distance reward, schema gating and a capped length penalty. SFT and RL use 7,172 English NLP training instances; the main test has 1,740 instances across 16 scientific domains. In Table 1, the Qwen3-8B no-thinking model reaches judged Creative Utility 0.64 versus 0.21 after SFT and 0.38 with impact-only RL; idea distance is 0.88 versus 0.38 for impact-only RL. Grounding falls from 0.90 after no-thinking SFT to 0.61 after RL; the thinking variant trades lower utility (0.51) for higher grounding (0.81). The four-expert, 60-instance human pilot reports 2.17 promising ideas per set versus Claude’s 2.20. Appendix F’s execution pilot has 15 source instances (14 for the thinking variant), using a budgeted coding agent and its own experimental verdicts, not independently validated scientific discoveries. The author-linked repository currently contains only a coming-soon README. First inspected during this run; the paper is an unreported October 16 new-submission batch contribution inside the 72-hour lookback, so it is a delayed discovery rather than an October 18 release. Original October 15 receipt date is retained.

**Limitations:** All results are author-reported. LLM judges define quality, distance, grounding and most benchmark outcomes; a 2026 test-year split alone does not prove absence of training contamination. The within-set reward does not ensure diversity across the population: IdeaSeed method-type entropy is 0.65 for no-thinking and 0.73 for thinking, below the reported human 0.87. The DARLING comparison also changes initialization, rollout grouping and clipping, so it does not isolate only where diversity is rewarded; the impact-only ablation is the cleaner comparison. Four experts and 15 execution instances are small pilots, and the execution agent’s self-reported support/refutation is not verified discovery. Training uses an external distance-judge API in addition to the local H200 allocation. Code, data and models are promised, not released in the verified project. No broad scientific-discovery or universal SoTA claim is supported.

## [2026-10-14](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-14.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18853>)

Two Clocks separates the samples needed for learning progress from those consumed before training collapse when rollout batches and learning rates are scaled together. Its controlled GRPO experiments motivate starting below a critical batch size and increasing the batch later, helping practitioners evaluate sample efficiency and stability separately from hardware throughput.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:31.851Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** RLVR, Batch Scaling, Training Stability

**Public availability:** 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18853>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Availability is inferred from the October 14 primary-category new-submission batch and official schedule. Sections 3–6 and Appendices B, F and G test 512–8,192-response batches, clipping and batch ramps on Qwen math models; larger batches lose sample efficiency above a learning-rate-dependent critical scale.

**Limitations:** The local quadratic progress model and drift-threshold failure hypothesis are conditional approximations. Most runs use a modified 1.5B math recipe with KL, entropy bonuses and gradient clipping disabled; robustness settings have limited seeds. The author-linked code repository returned 404, and no end-to-end throughput gain was established.

### [When KL Regularization Misfires in Group Policy Optimization](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12161>)

ZCPO folds length-normalized, group-centered policy divergence into frozen response-level update coefficients instead of adding a separate KL penalty. This makes reference-policy guidance interact with the same update controls as reward feedback, improving the tested reasoning and long-context training runs.

## [2026-10-07](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-07.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [TRACE: Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training for FP4 Reinforcement Learning of MoE Language Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07767>)

TRACE uses recorded rollout quantization outcomes to guide training-time FP4 rounding, compressing the guidance to mantissa bits and scales from later layers. This reduces train-rollout mismatch in the tested MoE reinforcement-learning runs, helping preserve model quality while exploiting cheaper low-precision generation.

**Published:** 2026-10-06 · **First seen:** 2026-10-07T10:09:33Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Quantization-Aware RL, FP4, Policy Consistency

**Public availability:** 2026-10-07T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07767>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Four Qwen MoE models span reasoning, coding and long-horizon tasks. The 35B model averages 75.3 versus BF16's 74.9 and ordinary QAT's 59.6. Its rollout reaches up to 5.4 times BF16 throughput at 128K outputs on four GB200s; RL step overhead versus vanilla joint FP4 is 7.4%. Original v1: 2026-10-06T05:03:47Z; public batch inferred from October 7's listing.

**Limitations:** The speedup is for decoding, not total training. Only routed experts and attention KV are quantized; backward remains BF16. Exact-codeword guidance has a local guarantee that does not extend to global policy divergence, and compressed guidance is approximate. Results are author-run point estimates; no author implementation was verified.

## [2026-10-06](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-06.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06647>)

LoGRA accumulates gradients directly into low-rank sketches, optimizes the sketches, and applies their reconstructed updates to selected full-weight matrices during language-model RL. Combining compressed optimizer state and rollout synchronization with a predicted-KL step controller substantially reduces training memory while preserving the tested reasoning performance.

**Published:** 2026-10-05 · **First seen:** 2026-10-06T10:03:05Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** RL Optimization, Gradient Sketching, Training Memory

**Public availability:** 2026-10-06T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06647>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Three-seed Qwen experiments span 1.5B, 7B, and 27B models. At 7B, average allocated memory per training GPU falls from 31.82 to 17.29 GiB, while peak MATH500 pass@1 is 72.48% for dense Adam versus 72.33% for LoGRA. Original submission: 2026-10-05T16:28:11Z; the October 6 listing and official schedule establish the public batch at 00:00Z.

**Limitations:** The optimizer and KL control change together, and only selected matrices are trained. The local predicted-KL approximation is not a realized-KL guarantee. Throughput gains are modest; the long 27B run uses one trajectory. The paper-linked Molt implementation could not be accessed, so no code URL is asserted.

### [HuatuoGPT-3: RL-Only Domain Adaptation from Base Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05966>)

This report extends OnePO to medical domain adaptation, mixing rewarded teacher responses into RL groups only while they outperform the model's current samples and correcting weak gradients on unlikely teacher tokens. ## [2026-10-04](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-04.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02039>)

CARM filters RL training responses using the average absolute token log-probability ratio, preventing opposing policy changes from hiding one another through cancellation. It improves math and coding results in the tested GRPO runs while keeping the underlying token-level objective, providing a simple way to control response-level mismatch between rollout and training policies.

**Published:** 2026-10-01 · **First seen:** 2026-10-04T10:06:11Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** GRPO, Off-Policy Correction, Response Filtering

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02039>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Experiments compare five masking choices with Qwen3.5-4B/9B and three seeds; the 9B four-benchmark math average rises from 67.29% with GeoMean to 70.42% with CARM. Submission: 2026-10-01T16:51:56Z; the cs.CL listing confirms the October 2 public batch. Newly discovered in this run's lookback, absent from the registry.

**Limitations:** Thresholds are swept and checkpoints selected using AIME or LiveCodeBench validation scores, limiting claims of untouched-test generalization. The bound concerns sampled-token mismatch, not full-distribution divergence or guaranteed stability. Filtering occurs after response generation and does not establish rollout-cost savings. Evidence is limited to one model family; no author implementation URL was verified.

## [2026-10-03](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-03.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Make Sparse Rewards Count: Density-Aware Reward Aggregation for Multi-Reward RL](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00574>)

Density-Aware Reward Aggregation increases the weight of objectives that provide useful comparisons in relatively few rollout groups, recalculating these weights for each training batch. This helps models acquire format and length constraints in fewer optimization steps, offering a practical way to balance multiple rewards while exposing the trade-off between compliance and answer accuracy.

**Published:** 2026-09-30 · **First seen:** 2026-10-03T10:04:50Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Multi-Reward RL, Advantage Weighting, Training Efficiency

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00574>) · [Code](<https://github.com/zhaihaotian/DARA>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Tool-calling and math studies cover 1.5B–7B models, matched baselines, fixed-weight ablations, and held-out evaluation. DeepSeek-R1-7B reaches 95% held-out length compliance at step 50 versus 70 for GDPO. Submission: 2026-09-30T18:45:26Z, after the daily deadline; the cs.CL listing confirms the October 2 public batch. Newly discovered in this run's lookback, with the September 30 original date retained.

**Limitations:** Fewer optimization steps do not establish wall-clock savings. Stronger length compliance can lower accuracy, and final accuracy leadership varies by model and variant. The exact energy-equalization result assumes ideal normalization and uncapped symmetric weights; it does not directly prove equal policy-gradient contributions for the practical asymmetric variant.

## [2026-10-01](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-01.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Learning Beyond What You Sample: Off-Policy-Aware Cross-Model Trajectory Exchange for RLVR](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37868>)

GRAFT replaces a learner's entirely unsuccessful rollout groups with informative groups from a peer model, controlling policy mismatch through compatibility weighting and clipped updates. This lets heterogeneous models learn from complementary discoveries without a designated stronger teacher, and stored peer trajectories can retain much of the benefit.

**Published:** 2026-09-29 · **First seen:** 2026-10-02T15:32:39Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** RLVR, Trajectory Sharing, Off-Policy Learning

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37868>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Three model pairs and five math benchmarks show average gains of about 2.1 points over eight-rollout GRPO; ablations test gating and group replacement. arXiv v1: 2026-09-29T15:47:25Z. Newly discovered through the September 30 discovery index during this delayed run, within the 72-hour lookback and absent from prior reports. The timestamp above is submission time; the arXiv recent-submissions listing separately confirms the September 30 public announcement batch.

**Limitations:** Experiments use two-model pairs of at most 3B parameters on verifiable math. Gains depend on complementary successes, cross-tokenizer weights are compatibility proxies rather than exact density ratios, and paired-training compute should not be presented as a single-model cost reduction.

DeepSeek-R1 demonstrates large-scale reasoning training with group-relative policy optimization and verifiable rewards, while separating a pure-RL experiment from a staged recipe that improves response usability. It supplies a foundational reference for eliciting reasoning from a strong pretrained model and transferring those capabilities to smaller models through distillation.
